"## ISO 17100 translation services standard: core requirements, translator competencies, and mandatory quality assurance/revision steps
# ISO 17100:2015 — Translation Services Standard

**ISO 17100:2015 "Translation services — Requirements for translation services"** was published in May 2015 (developed by ISO/PC 232) and superseded the earlier European standard EN 15038:2006 as the international benchmark. It specifies requirements for all aspects of the translation service delivery process by a Translation Service Provider (TSP) and applies to **human translation only** — raw machine translation output without human intervention is out of scope (post-editing of MT is covered separately by ISO 18587:2017) [1].

## 1. Core Requirements

- **Documented management system** for translation service provision, covering workflow, responsibilities, and record-keeping.
- **Defined roles**: translation service coordinator/project manager, translator, reviser, reviewer, and proofreader — each with specified competence requirements.
- **Client-facing processes**: quotation, a documented service agreement capturing project specifications (target language/locale, deadline, deliverables, terminology, style, domain, etc.), and client confirmation before production.
- **Project preparation and tracking**: feasibility assessment, resource assignment, technical preparation, and monitoring throughout production.
- **Technical resources**: appropriate tools (CAT/terminology management), secure handling, storage, and backup of client data.
- **Confidentiality**: non-disclosure agreements with clients and all personnel; data protection obligations.
- **Subcontracting** is permitted, but the TSP retains full responsibility and must ensure subcontractors meet the same requirements.
- **Post-production**: client feedback collection, complaint/nonconformity handling, and project closure [1][2].

## 2. Translator Competencies

The standard defines **five core competencies** every translator must possess [1]:

1. **Translation** — ability to conduct the full translation process to meet project specifications
2. **Linguistic and textual** — command of grammar, syntax, semantics, style, register, and text-type conventions in both source and target languages
3. **Research, information extraction and processing** — ability to acquire terminology/subject-matter knowledge and use reference materials and tools
4. **Cultural** — knowledge of source and target locale conventions, norms, and values
5. **Technical** — proficient use of translation technology and tools

(Domain/subject-matter competency is an additional, context-dependent competency.)

**Qualification evidence** — translators must demonstrate **at least one** of the following [1]:
- A formal higher education qualification in translation; **or**
- A higher education qualification in any other field **plus 2 years' full-time professional translation experience**; **or**
- **5 years' full-time professional translation experience**.

**Other personnel**: revisers need translator-level competencies **plus professional translation experience**; reviewers need domain expertise; proofreaders need target-language competence; project managers need knowledge of the translation workflow [1][2].

## 3. Mandatory Quality Assurance / Revision Steps

ISO 17100 enforces a **two-person principle**: translation and revision must be performed by different people [1][3].

| Step | Status | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Translation | Mandatory | Performed by a qualified translator |
| **Check** | Mandatory | Translator's self-examination of the target text against the source |
| **Revision** | **Mandatory** | Independent second person compares target vs. source for completeness, accuracy, terminology, and conformity with specs; recommends corrective action |
| Review | Optional (if agreed) | Assessment of fitness for purpose in the domain, terminology correctness, and register — requires domain expertise |
| Proofreading | Optional (if agreed) | Pre-delivery check for typos, omissions, and formatting errors |
| **Final verification and release** | Mandatory | Designated person verifies the deliverable against agreed specifications before release |
| Delivery & feedback | Mandatory | Delivery, client feedback evaluation, complaint handling |

**Key point**: only the translator self-check, independent revision, and final verification/release are obligatory for every project; review and proofreading are value-added steps performed when specified in the service agreement [1][3].

TSPs can be third-party certified against ISO 17100 by accredited certification bodies.

---
*Note: No live search results were returned in this session; the above reflects the published text of the standard and its widely documented summaries. Key references: [1] ISO 17100:2015, ISO.org (standard 59149); [2] GALA — "ISO 17100" overview; [3] ISO 17100:2015 Clause 6 (production process: check, revision, review, proofreading, final verification).*

## Standard components of a professional translation brief or translation contract: scope, deliverables, terminology management, review and revision workflow
# Standard Components of a Professional Translation Brief / Contract

The components below reflect the main industry frameworks: **ISO 17100:2015** (translation services requirements) [1], **ASTM F2575** (Standard Guide for Quality Assurance in Translation) [2], and the **European Commission DGT translation brief model** [3], supplemented by common terms of business used by professional associations (ATA, ITI, ELIA) [4].

## 1. Scope
- **Languages and directions** (e.g., EN→DE only, not reverse), subject-matter domains (legal, medical, technical, marketing), and text types (contracts, manuals, web copy).
- **Service definition**: translation only vs. full TEP (translation–editing–proofreading), machine-translation post-editing (MTPE), transcription, DTP/layout, software/website localization, subtitling, sworn/certified translation — and explicit **exclusions**.
- **Volume and pricing basis**: word counts, unit of count (source vs. target words), rates per word/hour/project, minimum fees.
- **Purpose, audience, and register**: ASTM F2575 and the DGT brief both require stating the intended function of the target text and its target audience, since quality is defined as conformance to agreed specifications [2][3].
- **Source material condition**: editable files vs. scans/handwriting, completeness, legibility; assumptions made.
- **Deadlines, milestones, partial deliveries**, and a **change-control procedure** (out-of-scope changes trigger re-quotation).
- **Confidentiality and data-protection requirements** (NDA, GDPR, secure file transfer).

## 2. Deliverables
- **Output formats**: same format as source (DOCX, IDML, JSON, XLIFF), or specified alternatives; QA/error reports if promised.
- **Project assets**: translation memory (TM), termbase/glossary, style guide — with explicit **ownership and licensing terms** (client-owned vs. provider-owned).
- **Certification or sworn statements** where legally required.
- **Delivery method, acceptance window, and acceptance criteria** (e.g., client has 10 business days to review; silence constitutes acceptance).
- **Invoicing documentation** tied to the agreed unit of count.

## 3. Terminology Management
- **Glossary/termbase creation** before production: key terms, definitions, approved target equivalents; **client validation** of the glossary as a project milestone.
- **Do-not-translate lists**, brand names, product names, and legacy terminology from previous translations.
- **CAT-tool consistency enforcement** and TM leverage; ISO 17100 requires the provider to verify terminology appropriateness and domain conventions as part of project preparation and translation [1].
- **Maintenance responsibilities** during and after the project, and who may add/modify entries.

## 4. Review and Revision Workflow
- **Defined process steps**. ISO 17100 specifies: translation → self-check by the translator → **revision** (bilingual check of target against source for completeness/accuracy by a second qualified linguist) → optional **review** (monolingual check of fitness for purpose) → optional **proofread** (final check before publication) [1]. The commercial equivalent is the "TEP" model.
- **Number of revision rounds included** in the fee; how client feedback is consolidated (single-channel feedback, tracked changes).
- **Automated QA checks** (terminology consistency, numbers, tags) via QA tools.
- **Acceptance and complaint handling**: rectification obligations for genuine errors within a defined period; post-acceptance changes treated as chargeable change requests.
- **Reviewer qualifications**: ISO 17100 requires revisers to meet the same competence criteria as translators plus experience in the domain [1].

## Other Standard Contract Clauses (brief)
- IP rights/copyright assignment or license in the translations; confidentiality surviving termination; liability caps (commonly limited to fees paid); payment terms (e.g., net 30, deposits for new clients); cancellation fees; non-solicitation; dispute resolution/governing law [4].

**Key principle across frameworks**: quality disputes are adjudicated against the *written specifications* agreed in the brief/contract, so the four areas above should be documented before work begins [1][2][3].

---
**Sources**
[1] ISO 17100:2015, *Translation services — Requirements for translation services*
[2] ASTM F2575, *Standard Guide for Quality Assurance in Translation*
[3] European Commission Directorate-General for Translation (DGT), *Translation Brief* framework
[4] Professional association guidance on terms of business (American Translators Association; Institute of Translation and Interpreting; ELIA)

## Best practices for adapting locale-specific conventions in translation: dates, numbers, currency, units of measure, punctuation and typography
# Locale Adaptation Best Practices: Research Summary

## Core principles
- Format decisions must key on **locale, not language**: pt‑BR and pt‑PT, en‑US and en‑GB differ substantially in dates, numbers, and units [1][2].
- Never hardcode formats. Use locale-aware libraries (ICU, Java/.NET formatters, ECMAScript `Intl`) backed by the **Unicode CLDR** as the canonical data source for date, number, currency, and unit patterns [2][8].
- Internationalize first: externalize all strings and locale-sensitive data so translators and formatters—not code—control conventions [4][5][11].

## Dates and times
- Component order varies: MDY (en‑US), DMY (most of Europe/Latin America), YMD (East Asia); separators vary too (German uses dots: 31.12.2025) [1][2].
- Use spelled-out month names where ambiguity matters; use **ISO 8601 (YYYY‑MM‑DD)** for technical/machine-readable contexts [6].
- Account for first day of week (Sunday vs. Monday vs. Saturday), 12‑hour vs. 24‑hour clocks, and non-Gregorian calendars (Buddhist in Thailand, Hijri, Japanese eras) [2][8].
- Handle time zones and DST via libraries, never manual offsets [8].

## Numbers
- Decimal/group separators swap between locales: 1,234.56 (en‑US) vs. 1.234,56 (de‑DE, pt‑BR); French uses a narrow no-break space (1 234 567,89); Swiss German uses an apostrophe (1'234'567) [2][8].
- Grouping is not always by thousands: India uses lakh/crore grouping (12,34,56,789) [2].
- Some locales use non-Western digit shapes (Arabic-Indic, Devanagari, Thai) [2].
- Percent-sign spacing/placement varies (French: "50 %") [2].

## Currency
- Symbol position and spacing vary: $1,234.56 vs. 1.234,56 € vs. 1 234,56 € — apply via CLDR currency patterns, not string concatenation [2][8].
- Symbols are ambiguous across markets ($ = USD/CAD/AUD/MXN; kr = SEK/NOK/DKK); use **ISO 4217 codes** (USD, EUR, JPY) when disambiguation matters [7][15].
- Minor-unit digits differ: JPY has 0, most currencies 2, KWD/BHD have 3 — don't assume two decimals [2][7].

## Units of measure
- Convert **values**, not just symbols: metric vs. US customary vs. mixed UK usage (miles for distance, Celsius for temperature, stone for body weight) [1][3].
- SI rules: a (non-breaking) space between value and unit symbol (25 kg, 300 mL); no space after the degree sign (20 °C uses a space, but angles like 45° do not) [9].
- Localize ancillary formats too: paper sizes (A4 vs. US Letter), clothing/shoe sizes, address and phone formats [3][11].
- Unit mismatches cause real failures — e.g., the 1999 loss of NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter to a metric/imperial mix-up; verify all converted figures [10].

## Punctuation and typography
- Quotation marks differ: “ ”/‘ ’ (English), « » (French, Spanish, Russian, pt‑PT), „ “ (German), 「 」 (Japanese), 《 》 for titles in Chinese [2][11][12].
- French requires non-breaking spaces inside guillemets and before ; : ! ? [2].
- Spanish uses inverted ¿ ¡ [11].
- Capitalization conventions differ: English title case vs. sentence case elsewhere; German capitalizes all nouns; Arabic, Hebrew, CJK, and Devanagari have no case — avoid ALL-CAPS styling assumptions [3][11].
- Line breaking: CJK follows kinsoku (forbidden break) rules; Thai, Lao, Khmer, and Myanmar have no inter-word spaces and need dictionary-based breaking (ICU) [8][12].
- **Text expansion/contraction**: German runs ~30% longer than English; CJK often shorter — build flexible layouts [3][4].
- Bidirectional scripts (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu) require RTL layout, the Unicode Bidi Algorithm, and mirrored punctuation [13][14].

## Process and QA
- Run **pseudo-localization** to expose hardcoded formats, truncation, and expansion issues before translation [4][11].
- Follow published per-language style guides (Microsoft, Google, Apple) and the EU Interinstitutional Style Guide for pan-European consistency [3][4][5][15].
- Use CAT-tool automated QA checks for number/date/currency consistency and have in-country (native) reviewers validate final formatting [3][11].

## Handling untranslatable elements in professional translation: placeholders, markup tags, code snippets, URLs, proper nouns, and terminology consistency rules
# Handling Untranslatable Elements in Professional Translation

## Placeholders
- Tokens such as `%s`, `{0}`, `{{user_name}}`, and `$1` must be preserved verbatim; translators may reposition them to match target-language word order, which requires *positional/numbered* placeholders (e.g., `%1$s` in Android, `{0}` in .NET) rather than sequential ones [6][8].
- ICU MessageFormat is the standard for complex cases (pluralization, gender) where placeholder selection varies by locale [6].
- CAT tools treat placeholders as protected "placeables" that are copied, not typed, and QA checks flag missing, extra, or corrupted tokens [9][10].
- In machine translation pipelines, placeholders are masked or tokenized so MT cannot alter them [7].

## Markup Tags
- Inline HTML/XML tags are locked as paired units; QA validation detects deleted, added, illegally reordered, or split tags [2][10].
- XLIFF 2.x models inline content with elements such as `<ph>`, `<pc>`, and `<sc>`/`<ec>` so tools can enforce tag integrity across systems [2].
- The W3C ITS (Internationalization Tag Set) defines data categories like "Translate / Do Not Translate" and "Within Text" to declare which markup nodes are translatable [1].

## Code Snippets
- Best practice is *string externalization*: separating user-facing text into resource files (gettext `.po`, `.resx`, `.strings`, JSON) so code and translatable content never mix [14][8].
- Identifiers, function names, API keys, and CLI flags remain in the source language; only string literals and comments are translation candidates [8].
- In documentation, code blocks are typically locked or marked DNT ("do not translate") in the CAT tool [9][7].

## URLs
- URLs are non-translatable placeables — altering them breaks links — so they are protected or inserted as tags [9][10].
- Localized domains and paths (IDN domains, locale directories such as `/de-de/`) are editorial/SEO decisions, not translation tasks [11].
- `hreflang` annotations signal language/region targeting between localized page versions [11].

## Proper Nouns
- Default rule: personal and organization names are not translated; different scripts use transliteration standards (ISO 9 for Cyrillic, Hanyu Pinyin for Chinese, UNGEGN systems for geographic names) [12].
- Exceptions governed by style guides/termbases: conventional exonyms (e.g., Germany/Allemagne), officially localized brand and product names, and established local forms of entity names [4][5].
- DNT lists lock specific terms from translation and MT post-editing [7][9].

## Terminology Consistency
- Termbases in **TBX** format (ISO 30042) store approved source–target term pairs, definitions, and status; translation memories in **TMX** store validated segment pairs [3].
- CAT tools enforce consistency through termbase recognition, term highlighting, and automated terminology QA (missing term, forbidden term, inconsistent rendering) [9][10].
- Client style guides (e.g., Microsoft Writing Style Guide, Google Developer Documentation Style Guide) define casing, capitalization, and when product names may be translated [4][5].
- Dedicated QA tools such as Xbench and Verifika run cross-file terminology and consistency checks before delivery [13].
- Working rule: one approved target term per source term per product/context; any deviation requires documented approval in the termbase [3][13].

**Typical workflow:** pre-extract strings and lock non-translatables (code, tags, URLs, DNT terms) → translate with termbase and TM support → run automated QA (placeholders, tags, terminology) → human review against the style guide [1][2][9][10][13].
